Minkowski addition adds support functions, so insert $h+tk$ into the area identity:
$$A(K+tL)=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(h^2-h'^2)\,d\theta+t\int_0^{2\pi}(hk-h'k')\,d\theta+\frac{t^2}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}(k^2-k'^2)\,d\theta.$$
Comparison with the specified coefficient $2tA(K,L)$ proves the formula and fixes its normalization. Symmetry in $h,k$ is immediate.

Translating $K$ by $v$ replaces $h$ by $h+f$, where $f(\theta)=v\cdot(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and $f''=-f$. Periodic integration by parts gives
$$2\,\Delta A(K,L)=\int_0^{2\pi}(fk-f'k')\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}(f+f'')k\,d\theta=0.$$
Symmetry handles translation of $L$. There are no endpoint terms because all functions are $2\pi$-periodic. For nonsmooth bodies the corresponding formula is $2A(K,L)=\int h_K\,dS_L$, with $S_L$ the boundary-length measure on normal directions; the derivative expression also extends to Lipschitz support functions by approximation.

First suppose the bodies are smooth. Integration by parts gives
$$A(K',L)-A(K,L)=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(h_{K'}-h_K)(h_L+h_L'')\,d\theta.$$
Inclusion is equivalent to $h_K\leq h_{K'}$, while $h_L+h_L''\geq0$ is the curvature-radius density, so the difference is nonnegative. If this density is everywhere positive, a proper inclusion gives a strict inequality: the continuous support difference is positive on some interval. Mere smooth strict convexity should not be confused with an everywhere positive density; the nonnegative argument is sufficient for monotonicity.

For general bodies, convolve both $h_K$ and $h_{K'}$ with the same nonnegative smooth approximate identity on the angle circle, then add the same small positive constant. These operations are Minkowski averages of rotations followed by disk addition, so they produce support functions, preserve inclusion, and converge uniformly to the originals. Smooth $L$ in the same way. Continuity of mixed area passes the inequality to the limit. Symmetry gives monotonicity in the other argument. Strictness need not survive this passage: the triangle-to-hexagon plateau supplies explicit proper inclusions with equality.

solutions.body_md:
For the arc centered at vertex $x_i$, write $I_i$ for its closed interval of outward unit normals. By the constant-width pairing, the opposite interval $-I_i$ is exactly the normal cone of $P$ at $x_i$, restricted to the unit circle. Its two endpoint directions are the normals of the incident arcs at $x_i$. The corresponding tangent half-planes are among those defining $C$, and their boundary lines meet at $x_i$. Every direction in $-I_i$ is a positive linear combination of those endpoint directions, so their inequalities imply
$$h_C(u)=h_S(u)=x_i\cdot u\qquad(u\in-I_i).$$
Here $S\subset P\subset C$ supplies the opposite inequality. The tangent normals surround the origin, so $C$ is a bounded convex polygon.

The skeleton edge joining the endpoints of the arc centered at $x_i$ has outward normal $m_i$ at the midpoint of $I_i$. Therefore $h_{-C}(m_i)=h_C(-m_i)=h_S(-m_i)=h_{-S}(m_i)$. The edge formula, with $S$ as its polygon argument, gives
$$2A(S,-C)=\sum_i\ell_i h_{-C}(m_i)=\sum_i\ell_i h_{-S}(m_i)=2A(S,-S).$$

Let $E$ be the finite set of endpoint tangent normals. The endpoints of every corner-normal interval are also incident arc endpoints, and the opposite-interval pairing therefore gives $E=-E$. Every edge normal of $C$ belongs to $E$; at every direction in $E$, a defining tangent touches $P$ at an original vertex, so $h_C=h_S$. Thus every edge normal of $-C$ also belongs to $E$ and sees equal support values of $C$ and $S$. Applying the edge formula with polygon $-C$ yields $A(C,-C)=A(S,-C)$.

We have proved equality at the endpoints of
$$A(S,-S)\leq A(K,-K)\leq A(C,-C).$$
Monotonicity proves the plateau for all intermediate $K$, including $P$. Equality is determined by the finitely many normals in the polygon measures, not by equality of the whole bodies.
